definition: Stipulate means to demand or specify something formally as a required condition of an agreement or other binding document.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stipulate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stipulate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The novelist's will stipulated that her letters stay sealed for fifty years, and the archive has kept the term to the day.
Request is milder than stipulate: a request can be declined and the bargain rolls on, while a stipulated term is formally required — the deal does not close without it.
Dictate goes further than stipulate: a party who stipulates demands one term and negotiates the rest, while one who dictates sets every term and leaves the other side no say at all.

To specify is to state something exactly — a measurement, a date, a model number. Anyone can specify anything, and no agreement is needed anywhere. Stipulate adds the bargaining table: the named term becomes a formal condition, and the deal itself carries it.

To require is to make something necessary, from any direction — a law, a recipe, or plain circumstance can require things. Stipulate is requiring done inside an agreement: one party names the term, formally, and it binds as part of the deal.
to give up a requirement you were entitled to insist on

Stipulari kept to the contract table: beyond stipulate itself and its noun, stipulation, Latin's formal-promise verb built nothing else in everyday English — a two-word family, both still doing exactly their Roman job.
Stipulate means to demand or specify something formally as a required condition of an agreement or other binding document.

When the zoo agreed to host a pair of giant pandas, the lending country stipulated the terms in writing: a purpose-built bamboo grove, a veterinarian on staff around the clock, and the pandas' return within ten years.
The moment the zoo's budget plan trimmed the vet position, the agreement stalled until it was restored.
That is stipulating: not hoping, urging, or merely describing, but naming a term formally so the agreement itself carries it — no grove, no vet, no pandas.
And mind the sound-alike trap: speculate, its near-twin in rhythm, means to guess without solid evidence.
Stipulating is the opposite of guessing — a term nailed down in writing.
Stipulate is contract-table language: a party stipulates a term, or the document itself does — the charter stipulates, the policy stipulates — usually with that and often a must close behind.
Courtrooms give it a second, related job: lawyers stipulate to facts, formally agreeing to them so no one has to prove them.
And guard the sound-alike: speculate means to guess without solid ground, and stipulating is guessing's opposite — a term fixed in writing.

The town's oldest scholarship comes with strings that surprise every winner.
Its founder, a shipping clerk who never finished school, left the money in a trust -- and the trust papers stipulate three conditions.
Winners must study within two hundred miles, return each summer to tutor at the library, and write the trustees one letter a year.
A student who skips a condition does not get a warning; the payments simply stop, because the terms are part of the gift itself.
Lawyers for the trust say the old clerk understood bargains: he named his terms formally, and every scholar since has signed them.
